## Loading Data

```{r}
library(readr)
Insurance_data <- read_csv("InsuranceData_correctedcolumns.csv")
View(Insurance_data)
```

Summary stats and looking at target

Dataset: CPS Annual Social and Economic (March 2026) Supplement for DC

<https://data.census.gov/app/mdat/CPSASEC2026/table?cv=NOW_COV,A_SEX,LJCW,PRWKSTAT&rv=ucgid,A_HGA,PRDISFLG&vv=A_AGE,HUNDER18,FTOTVAL&wt=MARSUPWT&g=AwFm-BVBlBGWg>

Column codes: <https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/cps/techdocs/cpsmar26.pdf>

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

df <- Insurance_data |>  select(where(~ !all(is.na(.x))))

# dropping state since all are from DC 
df <- df|> select(-STATE)

# make rows into factors 
df <- df |> 
  mutate(
    NOW_COV  = factor(NOW_COV),
    A_SEX    = factor(A_SEX),
    LJCW     = factor(LJCW),
    PRWKSTAT = factor(PRWKSTAT),
    A_HGA    = factor(A_HGA),
    PRDISFLG    = factor(PRDISFLG)
  )

# rename columns for clarity, some are kept the same 
df <- df |>
  rename(
    # NOW_COV: 1 = covered, 2 = not covered 
    NOW_COV = NOW_COV, 
    
    # sex: 1 = Male, 2 = Female
    SEX = A_SEX,
    
    # class of longest job 
    # 0 = NIU, 1 = private, 2 = federal, 3 = state, 4 = local, 
    # 5 = self employed incorporated, yes, 6 = self employed incorporated, no or farm
    # 7 = without pay
    LONGEST_JOB_CLASS = LJCW,
    
    # full or part time work 
    # 00 = NIU, 01 = Not in labor force, 02 = FT hours (35+), usually FT
    # 03 = PT for economic reasons, usually FT, 04 = PT for non-economic reasons, usually FT
    # 05 = Not at work, usually FT, 06 = PT hrs, usually PT for economic reasons
    # 07 = PT hrs, usually PT for non-economic, 08 = FT hours, usually PT for economic reasons
    # 09 = FT hours, usually PT for non-economic reasons, 10 = Not at work, usually part-time
    # 11 = Unemployed FT, 12 = Unemployed PT
    FULL_PART_TIME = PRWKSTAT,
    
    # highest grade achieved 
    # 0 = Children, 31 = Less than 1st grade, 32 = 1st,2nd,3rd,or 4th grade
    # 33 = 5th or 6th grade, 34 = 7th and 8th grade, 35 = 9th grade
    # 36 = 10th grade, 37 = 11th grade, 38 = 12th grade no diploma
    # 39 = High school graduate - high school diploma or equivalent
    # 40 = Some college but no degree, 41 = Associate degree in college occupation program
    # 42 = Associate degree in college, 43 = Bachelor's degree, 44 = Master's degree, 
    # 45 = Professional school degree, 46 = Doctorate degree
    EDUCATION = A_HGA, 
    
    # disability 
    # -1 = NIU, 1 = Yes, 2 = No
    DISABILITY = PRDISFLG, 
    
    # age
    AGE = A_AGE,
    
    # Number of persons in household under age 18
    HUNDER18 = HUNDER18, 
    
    # Total family income 
    TOTAL_FAM_INCOME = FTOTVAL
  )


summary(df)

```

```{r}
# split into training and testing 
set.seed(123)

# want to use 80-20 split 
training_pct <- 0.8

# split the data 
Z <- sample(nrow(df), floor(training_pct * nrow(df))) 
df_training <- df[Z, ]
df_testing  <- df[-Z, ]

# view split 
nrow(df_training)
nrow(df_testing)

```

```{r}

summary(df_training)

target_tbl <- df_training |> 
  count(NOW_COV) |> 
  mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2))

print(target_tbl)


ggplot(target_tbl, aes(factor(NOW_COV), n, fill = factor(NOW_COV))) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n, " (", pct, "%)")), vjust = -0.4) + 
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("1" = "Covered", "2" = "Not Covered")) + 
  labs(title = "Target distribution", x = "NOW_COV", y = "Count")

#numeric pred. by summary group

df_training |> 
  group_by(NOW_COV) |> 
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_age = mean(AGE), median_age = median(AGE),
    mean_income = mean(TOTAL_FAM_INCOME), median_income= median(TOTAL_FAM_INCOME),
    mean_under18 = mean(HUNDER18)
  )
```

```{r}

# scatter plot of age vs income 

ggplot(df_training, aes(x = AGE, y = TOTAL_FAM_INCOME, color = NOW_COV)) + geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Age vs Total Income Colored by Coverage", 
       x = "Age", y = "Total Family Income") + 
  scale_color_manual(name = "Insurance Coverage", values = c("1" = "coral1", "2" = "cyan3"), labels = c("1" = "Covered", "2" = "Not Covered")) + 
  scale_size_manual(values = c("1" = 1.5, "2" = 6))

```

## Looking at which matter most

```{r}
#install.packages("randomForest")
library(randomForest)

rf <- randomForest(NOW_COV ~ ., data = df_training, ntree = 500, importance = TRUE)

imp <- importance(rf) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column("variable") %>%
  arrange(desc(MeanDecreaseGini))
print(imp)

ggplot(imp, aes(reorder(variable, MeanDecreaseGini), MeanDecreaseGini)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("1" = "Covered", "2" = "Not Covered")) + 
  labs(title = "Variable importance (random forest)", x = NULL,
       y = "Mean decrease in Gini")

top_vars <- head(imp$variable, 3)
print(top_vars)

for (v in top_vars) {
  cat("\n---", v, "---\n")
  
  if (is.numeric(df_training[[v]])) {
    # numeric: summary by target + boxplot
    print(df_training %>% group_by(NOW_COV) %>% summarise(
      min = min(.data[[v]]), median = median(.data[[v]]),
      mean = mean(.data[[v]]), max = max(.data[[v]])))
    
    p <- ggplot(df_training, aes(NOW_COV, .data[[v]], fill = NOW_COV)) +
      geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
      scale_x_discrete(labels = c("1" = "Covered", "2" = "Not Covered")) + 
      labs(title = paste(v, "by NOW_COV"), x = "NOW_COV")
    if (v == "FOTHVAL") p <- p + scale_y_continuous(trans = "pseudo_log")
    print(p)
    
  } else {
    # categorical: proportion table + stacked bar
    print(round(prop.table(table(df_training[[v]], df_training$NOW_COV), margin = 1), 3))
    
    print(ggplot(df_training, aes(.data[[v]], fill = NOW_COV)) +
            geom_bar(position = "fill") +
            labs(title = paste("NOW_COV proportion by", v),
                 subtitle = "1 = covered, 2 = not covered", x = v, y = "Proportion"))
    }
}
```

Our group will be using demographic and income features from the U.S. Census Bureau data to predict whether an individual has health insurance coverage. This is a classification problem as we are trying to create a model to predict whether a person either has or does not have health insurance coverage. We have a mix of quantitative and qualitative variables, with notable variables such as income, age, and number of persons in the household under age 18 as clear quantitative variables. We also have data on sex, labor force status, the longest job class held by a worker, educational attainment, and state, all of which are important qualitative features.

Model 1.) We will first fit a simple KNN model with cross validation using just our quantitative features to predict health insurance coverage status. This will be a simple starting point from which we can develop more complex models that incorporate our qualitative features.

Model 2.) We will then fit a standard logistic regression model using both our quantitative and qualitative features to predict whether someone has healthcare coverage, using stepwise and best subset selection to find the best models in both cases. We will also leverage cross validation to iteratively split the data into testing and training sets in order to best train our model and evaluate its performance.

Model 3.) We will then leverage bootstrap sampling along with our best logistic regression model to use sampling with replacement as a strategy to estimate our logistic regression model. This will allow us to determine the accuracy and variability of our estimates by constructing confidence intervals for our model estimates. By repeatedly resampling with replacement from the dataset, we are able to construct a sampling distribution that allows us to determine model accuracy and variability. 

Model 4.) We will finally leverage tree methods to predict whether someone has healthcare coverage. With tree methods we will also be able to use the full breadth of both our qualitative and quantitative features to create a robust model to predict healthcare coverage status.
